Counting Triangles

InductionAreaSequences
Game: A triangle cut into small triangles slowly turns into a square cut into small squares. Find out how many green triangles there are at the two ends.
How to play: Move the slider between "Square" and "Triangle", and change N to cut the sides into more parts. Count the green triangles each time.

Look for the math

Cut each side of a square into N equal parts and draw the lines across: N² small squares, as everyone expects. Do the same to a right isosceles triangle and you get small triangles. The surprise is that there are exactly N² of them as well.

Why the two counts agree

With the slider at "Square", each of the N² small squares has one green triangle, so there are N² green triangles. Move the slider: some triangles under the diagonal fade out while the same number appear above it. The test checked that the ones that stay put are exactly N(N+1)/2, the ones that fade are N(N-1)/2 and the ones that come in are N(N-1)/2. So the picture at "Triangle" has N(N+1)/2 + N(N-1)/2 = N² triangles too. Folding the square along the diagonal would lay the new triangles on top of the old ones.

Odd numbers

Lines parallel to the long side cut the triangle into strips. The strip at the corner has 1 triangle, the next one 3, then 5, and the one along the long side has 2N - 1. So 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2N - 1) = N²: the sum of the first N odd numbers. The test confirmed the strip sizes for every N up to 60 and the area N²/2 that the triangles fill. The same fact has a proof by induction: going from k to k + 1 adds the odd number 2k + 1, and indeed (k+1)² - k² = 2k + 1. And the two triangular numbers N(N+1)/2 and (N-1)N/2 add up to N², which is the same fact seen from the other side.

Set N to 1, then to 2, and slide. Which triangle never moves?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
